# AF 第五章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 5

[P01] As winter came, Mollie became more and more troublesome. She was late for work every morning and said she had overslept. She complained of strange pains, but she ate well. On every excuse she ran from work to the drinking pool, where she stood looking at her own reflection. But there were rumours of something worse. One day, Mollie walked happily into the yard, moving her long tail and chewing（咀嚼） hay. Clover took her aside（旁边）. "Mollie," she said, "I have something serious to say.

[P02] This morning I saw you looking over the hedge（树篱） between Animal Farm and Foxwood. One of Mr. Pilkington's men stood on the other side. I was far away, but I am almost sure I saw this: he was talking to you, and you let him stroke your nose. What does that mean, Mollie?" "He didn't! I wasn't! It isn't（不是） true!" cried Mollie, starting to prance about. "Mollie! Look me in the face. Do you give me your word of honour that man was not stroking your nose?" "It isn't true!" repeated Mollie, but she could not look Clover in the face. The next moment she galloped away into the field. A thought struck Clover.

[P03] She did not tell the others. She went to Mollie's stall（畜栏） and, without saying anything to the others, turned over the straw（稻草） with her hoof（蹄）. Under the straw was lump（块） sugar and ribbons（丝带） in different colours. Three days later Mollie was gone. For some weeks no one knew where she was. Then the pigeons said they saw her on the other side of Willingdon. She was between the shafts（车辕） of a red and black dogcart（狗车） outside a public-house. A fat man with a red face, in check breeches（马裤） and gaiters（绑腿）, was stroking her nose and giving her sugar.

[P04] Her coat was newly cut short and she had a bright red ribbon（丝带） on her forehead（额头） hair. The pigeons said she looked happy. No animal ever spoke of Mollie again. In January the weather turned very hard. The earth was like iron, and no work could be done in the fields. Many meetings were held in the big barn（谷仓）. The pigs spent their time planning the work for the next season. It was now accepted that the pigs, clearly cleverer than the others, should decide all farm questions. But their decisions had to be agreed by a majority（大多数） vote.

[P05] This plan would have worked if Snowball and Napoleon had not argued. They disagreed（不同意） at every point. If one suggested sowing（播种） more barley（大麦）, the other demanded（要求） more oats（燕麦）. If one said a field was right for cabbages, the other said it was useless（无用） except for roots. Each had his own followers（追随者）, and there were violent（暴力的） debates. At the Meetings Snowball often won over the majority by his brilliant（聪明的） speeches, but Napoleon was better at gathering（聚集） support between times.

[P06] He was very good with the sheep. Lately the sheep had started bleating "Four legs good, two legs bad" at any time, and often stopped the Meeting. They were most likely to burst（爆发） into it at key moments in Snowball's speeches. Snowball had studied old copies of the 'Farmer and Stockbreeder（饲养员）' from the farmhouse（农舍）, and was full of plans for new ideas. He talked cleverly about field drains（排水沟）, silage（青贮饲料）, and basic slag（矿渣）, and had made a plan for all the animals to drop their dung（粪便） right in the fields, at a different spot（地点） each day, to save carting it away.

[P07] Napoleon had no plans of his own, but he said quietly that Snowball's plans would come to nothing, and he seemed to be waiting for his moment. But of all their fights, none was so bitter as the one over the windmill（风车）. These two disagreed on every point where disagreement（分歧） was possible. In the long pasture（牧场）, not far from the farm buildings, there was a small hill, the highest point on the farm.

[P08] After looking at the ground, Snowball said this was the place for a windmill. It could run a dynamo（发电机） and give the farm electrical（电力的） power. This would light the stalls（畜栏） and warm them in winter. It would also run a circular（圆形的） saw, a chaff（谷壳）-cutter（切割机）, and an electric milking machine. The animals had never heard of this (the farm was old-fashioned and had only simple machines). They listened in surprise while Snowball painted pictures of wonderful machines. These machines would do their work while they ate grass at their ease, or improved their minds with reading and talking. Within a few weeks Snowball's plans were fully worked out.

[P09] The mechanical（机械的） details came mostly from three books that had belonged to Mr. Jones—'One Thousand Useful Things to Do About the House', 'Every Man His Own Bricklayer（砖匠）', and 'Electricity for Beginners（初学者）'. Snowball used as his study a shed that had once been used for incubators（孵化器）. It had a smooth wooden floor, good for drawing on. He stayed there for hours. He held his books open with a stone. He gripped（攫住） a piece of chalk between the knuckles（指关节） of his trotter（猪蹄）. He moved quickly to and fro（来回）, drawing line after line and making little whimpers（呜咽） of excitement. Slowly the plans grew into a complicated（复杂的） mass（大量） of cranks（曲柄） and cog（齿轮）-wheels. It covered more than half the floor. The other animals found it completely unintelligible（难懂的） but very impressive（令人印象深刻）.

[P10] They all came to see Snowball's drawings almost every day. Even the hens and ducks came, trying not to step on the chalk marks. Only Napoleon stayed away. He had said he was against the windmill from the start. One day, however, he came without warning to look at the plans. He walked heavily（沉重地） round the shed, looked closely at every detail, and snuffed（嗅） at them. Then he stood for a while, watching them from the corner of his eye. Suddenly he lifted his leg, urinated（撒尿） over the plans, and walked out without a word. The whole farm was deeply divided about the windmill.

[P11] Snowball did not deny that building it would be hard work. Stone would have to be carried and made into walls, then the sails, and cables（电缆） were needed. But he said it could all be done in a year. After that, he declared（宣布）, so much labour（劳作） would be saved that the animals would only need to work three days a week. Napoleon argued that the great need was to increase food production, and that if they wasted time on the windmill they would all starve（饿死） to death.

[P12] The animals split（分裂） into two groups. One group had the slogan, "Vote for Snowball and the three-day week." The other had "Vote for Napoleon and the full manger（食槽）." Only Benjamin did not join either group. He did not believe food would become more plentiful（丰富）, or that the windmill would save work. Windmill or no windmill, he said, life would go on as badly as always. Besides the fights about the windmill, there was the question of defending（保卫） the farm. Everyone knew the humans had lost the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚）, but they might try again to take back the farm and put Mr.

[P13] Jones. They had even more reason to try, because news of their defeat had spread across the countryside. It made the animals on nearby farms more restless（不安） than ever. As usual, Snowball and Napoleon did not agree. According to Napoleon, the animals must get guns and train to use them. According to Snowball, they must send out more pigeons and start uprisings（起义） on the other farms. One argued that if they could not defend（保卫） themselves, they would be conquered（征服）. The other argued that if rebellions（叛乱） happened everywhere, they would not need to defend themselves.

[P14] The animals listened to Napoleon first, then to Snowball. They could not decide who was right. In fact, they always agreed with the one who was speaking at that moment. At last the day came when Snowball finished his plans. On Sunday at the Meeting, they would vote on whether to start work on the windmill. The animals gathered（聚集） in the big barn. Snowball stood up and gave his reasons for building the windmill. The sheep bleated and interrupted（打断） him sometimes.

[P15] Then Napoleon stood up to reply. He said quietly that the windmill was nonsense（胡说） and nobody should vote for it. Then he sat down. He had spoken for only thirty seconds. At this Snowball jumped to his feet. The sheep had begun to bleatagain（再次咩咩叫）, and he shouted them down. Then he made a strong, warm speech for the windmill. Until now the animals had been about equally divided, but in a moment Snowball's words carried them away. In bright sentences he painted a picture of Animal Farm as it might be when the hard labour was lifted from the animals' backs.

[P16] His imagination had now gone far beyond chaff-cutters（切割机） and turnip（萝卜）-slicers（切片机）. Electricity, he said, could run threshing（打谷） machines, ploughs, harrows（耙）, rollers（滚筒）, and reapers（收割机） and binders（捆扎机）. It could also give every stall its own electric light, hot and cold water, and an electric heater. When he finished speaking, no one doubted how the vote would go. But just then Napoleon stood up. He gave Snowball a strange sidelong（斜眼） look and let out a high-pitched（投掷） whimper（呜咽） of a kind no one had ever heard from him before. At this there was a terrible baying（吠叫） sound outside, and nine huge dogs with brass（黄铜）-studded（镶嵌） collars（项圈） came running into the barn.

[P17] They ran straight at Snowball. He jumped away just in time to escape their snapping（猛咬） jaws（嘴）. In a moment he was out of the door, and they ran after him. Too amazed and frightened to speak, all the animals crowded through the door to watch. Snowball was racing across the long pasture that led to the road. He was running as only a pig can run, but the dogs were close behind him. Suddenly he slipped（滑倒）, and it seemed certain that they had him. Then he was up again, running faster than ever, then the dogs were gaining on him again. One of them almost closed his jaws on Snowball's tail, but Snowball whisked（迅速移） it free just in time.

[P18] Then he ran faster for a moment and, with only a few inches to spare, slipped through a hole in the hedge and was seen no more. Silent and terrified（恐惧）, the animals crept（爬行） back into the barn. Soon the dogs came jumping back. At first no one could imagine where these animals came from, but the problem was soon solved: they were the puppies whom Napoleon had taken from their mothers and raised by himself.

[P19] Though not yet grown up, they were huge dogs, as fierce as wolves. They stayed close to Napoleon and wagged（摇摆） their tails to him, just as the other dogs used to do to Mr. Jones. Napoleon, with the dogs following, climbed onto the raised part of the floor where Major had stood. He said the Sunday-morning Meetings would end. They were not needed and wasted time. In future, all questions about the working of the farm would be decided by a special committee（委员会） of pigs, led by himself.

[P20] These would meet in private and then tell the others their decisions. The animals would still gather（收集） on Sunday mornings to salute（敬礼） the flag, sing 'animals of England', and receive their orders for the week; but there would be no more debates, and they were dismayed by Snowball's expulsion. The animals were shocked by Snowball's expulsion（驱逐）, and this announcement（宣布） dismayed（沮丧） them too. Several would have protested（抗议） if they could have found the right words. Even Boxer was vaguely（含糊地） troubled. He set his ears back, shook his forelock（额发） several times, and tried hard to gather his thoughts; but in the end he could think of nothing to say.

[P21] Some of the pigs themselves, however, could speak more clearly. Four young pigs in the front row let out loud, high squeals（尖叫） to show they did not agree, and all four of them jumped to their feet and began to speak all at the same time. But suddenly the dogs that sat around Napoleon gave deep, threatening（威胁的） growls（咆哮）, and the pigs became silent and sat down again. Then the sheep broke out into a tremendous（极大的） bleatingof（咩咩叫声） "Four legs good, two legs bad!" This went on for nearly a quarter of an hour and put an end to any chance of discussion.

[P22] Do not think, comrades（同志们）, that being a leader is fun! No, it is a heavy duty. No one believes more strongly than Comrade（同志） Napoleon that all animals are equal. He would be happy to let you decide things yourselves. But sometimes you might decide wrong, and then what would happen? What if you had followed Snowball, with his silly dream of windmills（风车） -- Snowball, who was just a criminal（罪犯）?""He fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚）," said somebody. "Bravery（勇敢） is not enough,"said Squealer. "Being loyal（忠诚） and obedient（顺从的） matters more. And one day we shall find that Snowball's part in the Battle was made to sound much bigger than it was.

[P23] Discipline（纪律）, comrades, iron discipline（纪律）! That is the watchword（口号） for today. One false step, and our enemies would be upon us. Surely, comrades, you do not want Jones back?" Once again this argument（争论） had no answer. Certainly the animals did not want Jones back. Certainly, if holding debates on Sunday mornings might bring Jones back, then the debates must stop. Boxer had now had time to think things over. Boxer voiced the general feeling: "If Comrade（同志） Napoleon says it, it must be right."And from then on he took the maxim（格言）, "Napoleon is always right," in addition to his own motto, "I will work harder." By this time the weather had broken and the spring ploughing had begun.

[P24] The shed where Snowball drew his windmill plans was closed, and everyone thought the plans were gone. Every Sunday at ten, the animals met in the big barn for orders. Old Major's skull（头骨）, now clean, was dug up from the orchard（果园） and put on a stump（树桩） by the flagstaff（旗杆）, next to the gun. After the flag went up, they walked past the skull with respect, then entered the barn. They no longer all sat together.

[P25] Napoleon sat at the front of the raised platform（舞台）, together with Squealer and another pig called Minimus, who had a wonderful gift for making up songs and poems. The nine young dogs formed a half-circle around them, and the other pigs sat behind them. The rest of the animals sat facing them in the main part of the barn. Napoleon read out the orders for the week in a rough, soldierly way, and after they sang 'Beasts（野兽） of England' just one time, all the animals went their separate ways.

[P26] He did not explain the change. He only warned that this extra（额外） work would be very hard, and they might even get less food. The plans were all ready, down to the smallest detail. A special committee of pigs had worked on them for three weeks. The windmill, with other improvements, would take two years. That evening Squealer told the animals in private that Napoleon had never really been against the windmill. On the contrary（相反的）, he was the one who had first spoken for it, and the plan Snowball had drawn on the floor was actually stolen from Napoleon's papers.

[P27] The windmill was, in fact, Napoleon's own idea. Why, then, asked somebody, had he spoken so strongly against it? Here Squealer looked very sly（狡猾的）. That, he said, was Comrade（同志） Napoleon's clever plan. He had SEEMED to oppose（反对） the windmill just to get rid of Snowball, a dangerous character and a bad influence. Now that Snowball was gone, the plan could go forward without his interference（干涉）. This, said Squealer, was something called tactics（策略）. He said again and again, "Tactics, comrades, tactics!" jumping round and moving his tail with a happy laugh. The animals were not sure what the word meant, but Squealer spoke so persuasively（有说服力）, and the three dogs with him growled（咆哮） so threateningly（威胁地）, that they accepted his explanation without more questions.
